title: UK butterflies did not recover after neonicotinoid-treated area fell by 80-92% in 2019-2024; the 1985-2012 neonicotinoid relation failed in national, country and site tests
abstract: Question: Gilburn et al. (2015) found that UK indices of 15 of 17 widespread butterflies were lower after years with large neonicotinoid-treated area (1985-2012). After the 2018 outdoor ban, did the indices increase as this relation predicts? Data: Fera Pesticide Usage Survey arable tables 2010-2024 (treated area 1.03-1.47 million ha to 2018, 0.09-0.25 million ha in 2020-2024); UKBMS 2024 collated and site indices; Met Office weather; ESA WorldCover cropland. Method: exact replication of the published mixed model; fit to 1985-2012 and one-step forecasts for 2013-2024 with and without the neonicotinoid term; England minus Scotland/Wales contrast; site test of post-ban change against cropland share within 2 km (1,170 transects, species x 100-km-square effects). Results: the replication matched (coefficient -0.065, published -0.064). The model predicted a mean rise of +0.158 log10 (about 44%) in 2021-2024 relative to 2013-2019; the observed change was -0.082 +- 0.047 (upper 95% limit 6% of the prediction), and the neonicotinoid model forecast worse than the model without it (RMSE 0.242 vs 0.148). No species reached its predicted rise. Fitted to 1985-2024, the coefficient changed sign (+0.017 +- 0.016). England gained +0.047 +- 0.016 relative to Scotland and Wales (predicted +0.24), but this continued a trend that started in 2010 while use was highest. Transects near cropland did not gain more: slope +0.036 +- 0.028 per 100% cropland against a dose-proportional prediction of +0.85. Conclusion: the 1985-2012 association is not causal at its published size. Limitations: 4 post-ban seasons; treated area is not toxicity; cropland share is a proxy; delayed recovery from persistent residues and effects on other taxa are not excluded.
